    Unit 1.1

    Opposite adjectives

    Theory

    1What are opposite adjectives?

    Adjectives describe people and things: tall, shy, noisy. Many adjectives come in pairs with opposite meanings (we call them antonyms). If Nam is talkative, he talks a lot — the opposite is quiet. Learning adjectives in pairs is a super trick: you learn two words at once!

    AdjectiveOpposite
    tall (tall)short (short)
    young (trẻ)old (già)
    noisy (ồn ào)quiet (yên lặng)
    generous (hào phóng)mean (keo kiệt)
    hard-working (chăm chỉ)lazy (lười biếng)
    brave (dũng cảm)cowardly (nhát gan)
    polite (lễ phép)rude (thô lỗ)

    2English in use

    My best friend Minh and I are complete opposites. He is talkative and brave; I am quiet and a little shy. His room is always tidy, but mine is messy. He is generous with his snacks — never mean — and though he is noisy in the playground, he is calm in exams. Opposites really do make the best friends!

    Worked example

    Example

    Read the sentence and find the opposite: “My grandma is quite serious, but my grandpa is very ______ — he tells jokes all day!”

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    The word but tells you the two people are different. Which adjective describes someone who tells jokes all day?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    funny. Serious ↔ funny are opposites: “…my grandpa is very funny — he tells jokes all day!”

    Practice

    Theory

    1Catching the key details

    When you listen for specific information, you don't need to understand every word! You only need to catch the key details: names, ages, numbers, days, places and spellings. Before listening: read the questions first and underline the key words. While listening: listen carefully for those words — the answer usually comes right next to them. Numbers and names are often repeated or spelled out, so you get a second chance.

    Question asks about…Listen for…
    Who? (ai?)names: Maria, Mr Lee…
    How old / how many?numbers: eleven, twenty-five…
    When? (khi nào?)days, months, times: on Monday, at 6 o’clock
    Where? (ở đâu?)places: at the library, in Da Nang

    2English in use

    Announcement: “The English Club meets on Thursday at 4.15 in Room 12B. Please tell Ms Lan — that's L-A-N — if you want to join. Bring 3,000 dong for the snack fund.” My notes caught only the key details: Thursday, 4.15, 12B, Lan, 3,000. I didn't understand every word — and I didn't need to!

    Worked example

    Example

    You will hear: “Hi, I'm Daniel — that's D-A-N-I-E-L. I'm eleven, and I go to swimming club on Thursdays.” The question asks: When does Daniel go to swimming club? What do you listen for? 🏊

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    The question word is When…? — so you need a day or a time, not a name or an age.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Listen for a day or time → the answer is on Thursdays. The name and the age are extra information you can ignore.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Adjective and preposition teams

    Some adjectives always work with a special preposition — they are a team, and you must learn them together. We say interested in music (never interested on), good at maths, afraid of spiders, proud of my sister, keen on football, kind to animals and famous for its beaches. After the preposition we use a noun (good at chess) or a verb with -ing (good at swimming).

    Adjective + prepositionExample
    interested inShe is interested in science.
    good / bad atI am good at drawing.
    afraid / scared ofHe is afraid of the dark.
    proud ofWe are proud of our school.
    keen onThey are keen on chess.
    kind toBe kind to animals.
    famous forHa Long Bay is famous for its islands.

    2English in use

    Let me introduce myself! I'm interested in dinosaurs and good at drawing them, though I'm still bad at spelling their long names. I'm a little afraid of thunder, but I'm never bored with rainy days — I just draw more! My parents are proud of my pictures, and I always try to be kind to my little sister when she borrows my pencils.

    Worked example

    Example

    Complete the sentence with the right preposition: “My best friend is really good ______ telling funny stories.”

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Which preposition is the partner of good? Also notice: telling ends in -ing — that's normal after a preposition.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    at — “My best friend is really good at telling funny stories.” Good always teams up with at.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Talking about habits and routines

    We use the present simple for things we do regularly: I get up at six. She walks to school. The magic rule: with he, she, it the verb gets -s (or -es): he plays, she watches, it rains. For negatives use don't / doesn't + base verb: I don't like tea. He doesn't like coffee (NOT doesn't likes). Frequency adverbs tell how often: always → usually → often → sometimes → never, and they go before the main verb: She always brushes her teeth.

    2English in use

    My sister Hoa has a perfect morning routine. She gets up at six and brushes her teeth while I still sleep. She walks to school with her friend, who carries the football. Classes start at seven fifteen. After school, Hoa practises piano, Dad cooks dinner, and the cat watches everything from the window. It never changes — and that's why it works!

    Worked example

    Example

    Make this sentence negative: “Minh plays video games on school nights.” 🏫

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Minh = he → use doesn't. Careful: after doesn't, the verb loses its -s!
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Minh doesn't play video games on school nights.” Doesn't + play (no -s), because doesn't already carries the he/she/it ending.

    Practice

    Theory

    1One paragraph, one idea

    A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea. The first sentence is often the topic sentence — it tells the reader what the paragraph is about; the other sentences add details. Start a new paragraph when you change to a new idea, a new time, a new place or a new person. Paragraphs make your writing easy to read — a text with no paragraphs is like a wardrobe with everything thrown on one shelf!

    2English in use

    Tết is my favourite holiday of the whole year. The streets fill with peach blossoms and red envelopes wait on every table. My grandmother cooks bánh chưng, and the smell drifts through the house for two whole days. Best of all, our faraway cousins finally come home. — Notice how the topic sentence announces one main idea, and every other sentence adds a detail about it!

    Worked example

    Example

    Linh is writing about her grandfather: first about his job, then about his hobbies. She has written 6 sentences with no breaks. Where should she start a new paragraph? ⭐

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Find the sentence where the topic changes from job to hobbies.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Start the new paragraph at the first sentence about his hobbies — that's where the main idea changes. Job = paragraph 1, hobbies = paragraph 2.

    Practice

    Theory

    1What makes a biography?

    A biography is the true story of a real person's life, written by someone else. Its special features: it is written in the third person (he/she, not I); it uses mostly the past tense (she was born…, he studied…); events come in time order with real dates and facts; and it often ends with why the person is important or remembered. (When a person writes about their own life, that's an autobiography.)

    2English in use

    Võ Thị Sáu was born in 1933 in Bà Rịa. She joined the resistance when she was only fourteen and became famous for her courage. In 1952, she died a hero, and today schools and streets across Vietnam carry her name. — Third person ✓, past tense ✓, real dates and achievements ✓, told by someone else ✓: every feature of a biography in four sentences!

    Worked example

    Example

    Read this opening: “Nguyễn Ngọc Ký was born in 1947 in Nam Định. When he was four, his arms became paralysed, so he learned to write with his feet.” Which biography features can you spot?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Look for: who is telling it (I or he?), the tense, and any dates or facts.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Third person (he), past tense (was born, became, learned), a real date (1947), a real place (Nam Định) and true facts — all classic biography features.

    Practice

    Theory

    1How to compare two poems

    When you compare poems, you look for what is the same and what is different. Compare these things: the theme (what the poem is about), the mood (happy? sad? funny?), the rhyme (do lines rhyme or not?), the rhythm (the beat) and the pictures the words paint. Useful comparing language: Both poems are about friendship. The first poem rhymes, whereas / but the second one doesn't. Unlike Poem A, Poem B is funny.

    2English in use

    I read two poems about rain this week. Both share the same theme — a storm — but their moods are opposites: the first feels playful and jumpy, while the second feels quiet and sad. The first rhymes in every line (drip/skip, pour/door); the second has no rhyme at all. Same subject, completely different music — that's what comparing poems shows you!

    Worked example

    Example

    Poem A is about a lost kitten and makes you feel sad. Poem B is about a naughty kitten and makes you laugh. Write ONE comparing sentence using both and one using but. 🐱

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Same thing: they are both about kittens (theme). Different thing: the mood (sad vs funny).
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Both poems are about kittens.” / “Poem A is sad, but Poem B is funny.” Same theme, different mood!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Words that rhyme

    Words rhyme when they end with the same sound: cat – hat, day – play, light – night. Watch out: rhyme is about sound, not spelling! Bear rhymes with chair (same sound, different spelling), but cough does NOT rhyme with through, even though both end in -ough. In a poem, we mark rhyming line-ends with letters — a rhyme scheme: if lines 1–2 rhyme and lines 3–4 rhyme, the scheme is AABB; if line 1 rhymes with line 3 and line 2 with line 4, it's ABAB.

    2English in use

    Listen to my tiny poem: “The cat in the hat sat down for a chat, / by day he would play, then dream the night away.” Cat–hat–chat rhyme, and so do day–play–away. But be careful: bear rhymes with chair even though the spelling is different, and through does NOT rhyme with tough — rhyme lives in the sound, not the letters!

    Worked example

    Example

    Find the rhyme scheme: “The moon is high (line 1) / The stars are bright (line 2) / I wave goodbye (line 3) / And say goodnight (line 4)” 🌙

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Say the last words aloud: high, bright, goodbye, goodnight. Which ones share a sound?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    High rhymes with goodbye (lines 1&3 = A) and bright rhymes with goodnight (lines 2&4 = B) → the scheme is ABAB.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Saying how you feel

    When you are ill, you can say what's wrong with I have (got) a…: I have a headache / a stomach ache / a sore throat / a cough / a cold / a fever (a high temperature) / a runny nose. To ask someone, say “What's the matter?” or “How do you feel?”. To wish them well: “Get well soon!” or “I hope you get better soon.”

    ProblemWhere it hurts
    a headache (đau đầu)head — đầu
    a stomach ache (đau bụng)stomach — bụng
    a sore throat (đau họng)throat — họng
    a toothache (đau răng)tooth — răng
    earache (đau tai)ear — tai

    2English in use

    At the doctor's: “What's the matter?” — “I have a headache and a sore throat, and last night I had a fever.” — “Any cough? A runny nose?” — “Just a small cough. My brother has a stomach ache too — maybe we both caught a cold at the pool!” — “Rest, warm water, and you'll feel better soon.”

    Worked example

    Example

    Bao's head feels hot, and the thermometer shows 39°C. What should he say to the doctor? 🩺

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    39°C is much higher than a normal body temperature (about 37°C). Which word means a high temperature?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “I have a fever.” (or “I have a high temperature.”) A fever means the body is hotter than normal.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Everyone, something, nowhere…

    Indefinite pronouns talk about people, things and places without naming them. Build them from every / some / any / no + -one/-body (people), -thing (things), -where (places): everyone, someone, anything, nothing, everywhere, nowhere… Rules: they take a singular verb (Everyone is here); use some- in positive sentences, any- in negatives and questions (I saw someone. I didn't see anyone. Did you see anything?); and no- words are already negative, so don't add “not” (Nobody came — NOT Nobody didn't come).

    PeopleThingsPlaces
    every-everyoneeverythingeverywhere
    some-someonesomethingsomewhere
    any-anyoneanythinganywhere
    no-no one / nobodynothingnowhere

    2English in use

    A classroom mystery! This morning someone left a gift on my desk, but nobody saw who. I asked everyone, and everybody shook their heads. I looked everywhere — under everything, behind the cupboard — but found nothing and nowhere to hide. Then Mai smiled… Is there anything she doesn't know? I don't think anyone keeps a secret from Mai!

    Worked example

    Example

    Complete: “I'm hungry, but there is ______ in the fridge!” (no + thing)

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    You need a THING word with a negative meaning — and remember, “is” stays positive because the no- word carries the negative.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “There is nothing in the fridge!” No + thing = nothing; the sentence needs no extra “not”.

    Practice

    Theory

    1The five food groups

    Scientists sort food into food groups, and a healthy plate takes something from each: fruit and vegetables (vitamins — apples, spinach); carbohydrates (energy — rice, bread, noodles, potatoes); protein (building muscles — fish, meat, eggs, beans, tofu); dairy (strong bones — milk, cheese, yogurt); and only a little fat and sugar (sweets, fried food). A balanced diet means eating from all the groups in the right amounts.

    GroupJobExamples
    Fruit & vegetablesvitamins, keep you healthybanana, carrot, spinach
    Carbohydratesgive you energyrice, bread, noodles
    Proteinbuild and repair musclesfish, eggs, beans, tofu
    Dairystrong bones and teethmilk, cheese, yogurt
    Fat & sugaronly a little!sweets, crisps

    2English in use

    Open my lunchbox and you'll find every food group! Rice for carbohydrates — my energy for the afternoon. Grilled fish and a boiled egg bring protein to help me grow. A little cheese adds dairy for strong bones, spinach and an apple pack in vitamins from the fruit and vegetables group, and just a tiny spoon of peanut oil covers the fats. A whole healthy plate in one box!

    Worked example

    Example

    Sort this lunch into food groups: rice, grilled fish, morning glory (rau muống), and a glass of milk. 🐟

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Ask each item: does it give energy, build muscles, give vitamins, or strengthen bones?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Rice = carbohydrates · grilled fish = protein · morning glory = vegetables · milk = dairy. Four groups on one plate — a balanced meal!

    Practice

    Theory

    1More, fewer, less, as many as

    Quantifiers compare amounts. First check the noun: countable (you can count them: apples, sweets) or uncountable (you can't: water, rice, sugar). Use more with both: more apples, more water. For smaller amounts: fewer + countable (fewer sweets), less + uncountable (less sugar). For equal amounts: as many … as (countable) and as much … as (uncountable): I have as many stickers as you. Drink as much water as you can.

    Countable (apples)Uncountable (water)
    moremore applesmore water
    fewer / lessfewer applesless water
    equalas many apples asas much water as

    2English in use

    Making fruit salad with Grandma: “We need more apples — and more sugar? No! There's already too much sugar and too many bananas. Use fewer bananas and less sugar, child. Is there enough milk for the cream? Hmm, a little milk, a few strawberries… perfect. Remember: we count strawberries, but we never count milk!”

    Worked example

    Example

    The doctor says: “Eat ______ sweets and ______ sugar!” Choose fewer or less for each gap. 🩺

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Can you count sweets (one sweet, two sweets)? Can you count sugar?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Eat fewer sweets and less sugar!” Sweets are countable → fewer; sugar is uncountable → less.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Advice vs rules

    Should gives advice — a good idea, but you can choose: You should drink more water. You shouldn't stay up late. Must is much stronger — a rule or obligation, no choice: You must wash your hands before eating. You mustn't run by the pool. Grammar rules for both: no -s with he/she/it (she must go — NOT musts), and the next verb is the bare infinitive without “to” (you should rest — NOT should to rest).

    2English in use

    Swimming pool rules and tips! Rules first — no choice: you must shower before entering, you must listen to the lifeguard, and you mustn't run on the wet floor. Now some friendly advice: you should bring goggles, you should drink water between races, and you shouldn't swim right after a big lunch. Rules keep you safe; advice keeps you happy!

    Worked example

    Example

    A sign at the pool says: “Children ______ wear armbands in the deep end.” Should we use should or must?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Is this friendly advice, or a safety rule with no choice?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    must — a pool sign is a safety rule, not a suggestion: “Children must wear armbands in the deep end.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1What makes a blog a blog?

    A blog is a personal website where someone writes regular posts. Its features: written in the first person (I/we) with a friendly, informal voice; each post has a title and a date, with the newest post first; posts often include photos, questions to the reader, and readers can leave comments. A health blog might share recipes, exercise tips or a story like “My week without fizzy drinks!”.

    2English in use

    My Week of Vegetables — Monday, 3rd March. Hi everyone! I've just finished day seven of my vegetable challenge, and honestly? I almost gave up at broccoli. 🥦 But morning glory with garlic — wow! Have you ever tried a food challenge? Tell me in the comments below, and click follow so you don't miss next week's post!

    Worked example

    Example

    Which text is from a blog? A: “Water boils at 100°C at sea level.” B: “Hi everyone! Guess what — I tried mango smoothies for breakfast all week. Have you ever tried one? Tell me in the comments!” 🥭

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Look for: first person (I), a chatty voice, a question to readers, and the word “comments”.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Text B: first person (“I tried”), informal (“Hi everyone! Guess what”), talks to readers and invites comments — classic blog features. A sounds like a science textbook.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Sorting things into groups with words

    When we classify, we sort things into groups — and English has special expressions for it: “A mango is a type of fruit.” “Rice belongs to the carbohydrate group.” “Dairy includes milk, cheese and yogurt.” “There are five kinds of food groups.” To give examples inside a group, use such as or for example: “Vegetables such as carrots and spinach are full of vitamins.”

    2English in use

    Sorting the shopping with Mum: “A mango is a type of fruit, so it goes with the apples. Rice belongs to the carbohydrate group — big basket! The dairy group includes milk, cheese and yogurt, so they sit together. And these? There are many kinds of noodles — phở, mì, miến — but they are all examples of carbohydrates too. Everything can be divided into groups — even a shopping bag!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Join the ideas with a classifying expression: “tofu / protein group” and give two more examples of that group.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Use “belongs to” for the group, then “such as” to add examples.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Tofu belongs to the protein group, which includes foods such as fish and eggs.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1Two different worlds

    The city is busy and modern: skyscrapers, traffic, shopping centres, museums, wide pavements and crowds of people. The countryside is calm and green: fields, farms, hills, forests, villages and fresh air. Useful describing patterns: “In the city there are lots of tall buildings.” “The countryside is much quieter than the city.”

    CityCountryside
    skyscraper (nhà chọc trời)field (cánh đồng)
    traffic (xe cộ đông đúc)farm (nông trại)
    shopping centre (TTTM)village (ngôi làng)
    museum (bảo tàng)hill (ngọn đồi)
    noisy, crowded (ồn ào, đông)quiet, peaceful (yên tĩnh, thanh bình)

    2English in use

    Postcard from my holiday: “Dear Lan, last week I was in the city — skyscrapers above me, traffic around me, crowds in the shopping centres, and a museum on every corner. Today I'm at Grandpa's in the countryside: green fields and rice paddies, quiet hills, a slow river, and buffaloes instead of buses! Busy and modern, or calm and green — which do you prefer?”

    Worked example

    Example

    Where does this sentence describe — city or countryside? “Every morning, the farmer walks past green fields and hears only birds singing.” 🐦

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Look for clue words: farmer, fields, birds singing (quiet!).
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    The countryside — farmer, green fields and quiet birdsong are all countryside clues.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Taller, more beautiful, the best

    Comparatives compare two things, with than: short adjectives + -er (taller than, bigger than — double the consonant in big→bigger), long adjectives use more (more beautiful than). Superlatives say which is top of the whole group, with the: the -est (the tallest) or the most (the most beautiful). Irregular stars to memorise: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst; far → farther → the farthest.

    AdjectiveComparativeSuperlative
    talltaller thanthe tallest
    bigbigger thanthe biggest
    noisynoisier thanthe noisiest
    beautifulmore beautiful thanthe most beautiful
    goodbetter thanthe best
    badworse thanthe worst

    2English in use

    Our geography quiz was full of comparisons! The Mekong is longer than the Red River, but the Nile is the longest river of all. Hà Nội is bigger than Huế, yet many say Huế is more beautiful than any city in Vietnam. Sơn Đoòng is the largest cave on Earth, my little brother thinks geography is the most boring subject — and I think it's better than maths, and maybe the best of all!

    Worked example

    Example

    Compare three cities: Hanoi (8 million people), Da Nang (1.2 million), Hue (0.5 million). Use big. 🦁

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Two cities → comparative (-er than). All three → superlative (the -est). Remember big doubles its g!
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Da Nang is bigger than Hue, but Hanoi is the biggest of the three.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1Being a reading detective

    Inference means working something out from clues, even when the text doesn't say it directly. When you are not 100% sure, use careful “maybe” language: could be, might be, perhaps, maybe, probably: “The streets are wet — perhaps it rained last night.” “This place has sand and palm trees. It could be a beach.” Only say must be when the clues make you almost certain.

    2English in use

    Detective notebook: “The kitchen window is open and there are muddy paw prints on the table. The thief could be an animal — perhaps the neighbour's cat. The fish is gone, so it must like seafood! It might have jumped in from the garden wall; it can't be the dog, because the prints are far too small. Probably, our thief is small, quick… and purring somewhere right now.”

    Worked example

    Example

    Read the clues: “In this place, people whisper. There are thousands of books on tall shelves, and a sign says Silence, please.” Where could it be? 📖

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Whispering + thousands of books + a silence sign… put the clues together.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    It must be a library — books, shelves and silence make it almost certain. (With fewer clues, you would say “it could be a library”.)

    Practice

    Theory

    1Fact or opinion?

    A fact can be checked and proved true: “Hanoi is the capital of Vietnam.” An opinion is what someone thinks or feels — different people can disagree: “Hanoi is the most exciting city in the world.” Opinion signals: I think, I believe, in my opinion, and judging adjectives like beautiful, boring, best, delicious. Ask the detective question: Can I check this in a book or with a measurement? Yes → fact. No, it depends on taste → opinion.

    2English in use

    From my book review: “The novel has 120 pages and was published in 2019 — you can check both, so those are facts. But when I write ‘I think the ending is the most exciting part’ and ‘In my opinion, the hero is too lucky’, those are opinions — my friend read the same book and believes the opposite! Facts can be proved; opinions can be debated.”

    Worked example

    Example

    Fact or opinion? A: “The Red River flows through Hanoi.” B: “The Red River is the prettiest river in Asia.”

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Which one can you check on a map? Which one depends on what a person finds pretty?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    A is a fact — check any map. B is an opinion — “prettiest” is a personal judgement; people can disagree.

    Practice

    Theory

    1First, next, then, finally

    Sequencing words put events in order, like signposts along a road: First, … Next, … Then, … After that, … Finally, … They usually stand at the start of the sentence with a comma: “First, we took the bus to the old town. Then, we visited the market. Finally, we watched the sunset by the river.” They make directions, stories and descriptions of a journey easy to follow.

    2English in use

    How I make the world's best instant noodles: “First, boil the water — really boiling, not just warm. Next, add the noodles and wait exactly three minutes. Then, stir in the seasoning. After that, crack an egg on top and cover the pot for one minute. Finally, add a few slices of chili and enjoy — my dad says the smell reaches the neighbours' house!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Put the trip in order with sequencing words: (visited the temple / packed our bags / arrived home / took the train) 🌧️

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    What must happen before you can travel anywhere? And what happens last?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “First, we packed our bags. Next, we took the train. Then, we visited the temple. Finally, we arrived home.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1Talking about yesterday

    The past simple describes finished actions. Regular verbs add -ed: visit → visited, play → played, stop → stopped, study → studied. Irregular verbs change completely — learn them by heart: go → went, see → saw, eat → ate, take → took, buy → bought, is/are → was/were. Negatives and questions use did + base verb: We didn't go. Did you see it? (the main verb goes back to its base form!).

    BasePastType
    visitvisitedregular
    studystudiedregular (y→i)
    gowentirregular
    seesawirregular
    buyboughtirregular

    2English in use

    Yesterday in my diary: “We visited Grandma and played cards all afternoon. She cooked phở, and I ate two bowls! Then we went to the lake, where I saw a huge turtle. Dad took a photo, my brother dropped his hat in the water, and everyone laughed. On the way home I bought ice cream and made a wish: more Sundays like this one.”

    Worked example

    Example

    Put the story in the past: “We go to Hoi An, see the lanterns and buy some cao lau noodles.” 🏮

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    All three verbs are irregular — no -ed anywhere!
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “We went to Hoi An, saw the lanterns and bought some cao lau noodles.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1Building a world with words

    A fictional place exists only in imagination — a floating city, a village inside a volcano! To make readers see it, describe it with the five senses: what you see (colours, shapes, sizes), hear, smell, feel and even taste. Use rich adjectives (glittering towers, misty forest), say where things are (in the middle stands…, behind the hills lies…) and add one magical detail that makes your place special: “In Cloudville, the houses hang from giant balloons, and it smells of rain and fresh bread.”

    2English in use

    Welcome to Cloudmarket, a town that floats above the sea! You see silver rooftops and balloons tied to every door; you hear wind-bells and the whoosh of flying boats. The air smells of rain and fresh bread, and the mist feels cool on your cheeks. Taste the famous cloud-candy — it melts before you chew! Five senses, one place that exists only in imagination.

    Worked example

    Example

    Improve this weak description: “The magic island is nice. It has trees.” 🌳

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Swap “nice” for a rich adjective, add a sense (sound? smell?) and one magical detail.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “The glittering island rises from a turquoise sea. Silver trees whisper in the wind, and the air smells of honey — because the rivers here flow with lemonade!”

    Practice

    Theory

    1Words for celebrations

    Special occasions have their own vocabulary: a festival (a big public celebration, like Tết or Diwali), a celebration, fireworks, a parade (people marching through the streets), decorations, costumes, presents/gifts, an invitation, and a tradition (something families repeat every year). Useful verbs: we celebrate Tết, we decorate the house, we invite our relatives, we give lucky money.

    2English in use

    Tết is the biggest festival of our year. We decorate the house with peach blossoms and traditional red banners, and on New Year's Eve the whole city watches the fireworks. There's a lion-dance parade through our street, families celebrate with a huge feast, children receive lucky money, and everyone wears their newest clothes for the special occasion.

    Worked example

    Example

    Describe Tết with three words from this lesson: what do you see in the sky, on the door, and in red envelopes?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Sky at midnight → f… ; things that make the house pretty → d… ; red envelopes hold a special present.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Fireworks light the sky, decorations (peach blossoms, kumquat trees) brighten the house, and the envelopes hold lucky money — a beloved tradition.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Who, which, where

    A defining relative clause glues extra information onto a noun to say exactly which one we mean. Use who for people: “The woman who makes bánh chưng is my aunt.” Use which (or that) for things and animals: “Tết is the festival which starts the lunar new year.” Use where for places: “This is the square where the fireworks explode.” Without the clause, the reader wouldn't know which woman, festival or square!

    2English in use

    Family photo tour! This is my aunt, the woman who makes the best bánh chưng in the district. Here's the kitchen where she works her magic, and the bamboo mould which belonged to her grandmother. That boy who is covered in flour? Me. And this is the photo that won our family competition — taken at the exact moment when the cake fell!

    Worked example

    Example

    Join the sentences with who/which/where: “That is the shop. We bought our lanterns there.” 🏮

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    A shop is a PLACE, and “there” disappears when you join the sentences.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “That is the shop where we bought our lanterns.” Place → where, and “there” is dropped.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Plans in the diary

    The present continuous (am/is/are + verb-ing) doesn't only describe now — it also talks about fixed future plans, things already arranged, often with a time word: “We are visiting grandma on Sunday.” “I'm wearing my áo dài tomorrow.” “Aunt Hoa is coming to the party next week.” Think of it as reading from the family calendar: the plan is decided, the date is set.

    2English in use

    Our weekend is fully booked! On Saturday morning we are visiting Grandpa, and at noon we are having lunch at the new noodle shop — Dad already reserved a table. In the afternoon my sister is playing in a chess tournament, so we are cheering for her. On Sunday my cousins are coming at nine, and that evening we are watching the fireworks together. Everything is arranged!

    Worked example

    Example

    Mai's diary for Saturday says: “10:00 — lion dance practice. 19:00 — dinner at Grandpa's.” Tell her plans using the present continuous. 🦁

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    The plans are fixed in the diary → am/is/are + verb-ing + time.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “On Saturday, Mai is practising the lion dance at 10:00, and she is having dinner at Grandpa's at 19:00.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1The trickiest letters in English

    The letters -ough look the same but sound completely different in different words — you must learn each word's sound: through (sounds like “throo”), enough and tough (“-uff”), thought and bought (“-ort”), although and dough (“-oh”), cough (“-off”). Fun sentence to practise: “Although I had a cough, I thought the party was fun enough!” — four different -ough sounds in one sentence!

    SoundWords
    “oo”through (xuyên qua)
    “uff”enough (đủ), tough (cứng rắn)
    “ort”thought (đã nghĩ), bought (đã mua)
    “oh”although (mặc dù), dough (bột nhào)
    “off”cough (ho)

    2English in use

    One letter-group, five sounds — read this aloud! “I thought I had bought enough flour, though the recipe was tough. The wind blew through the window and — achoo! — I started to cough.” Thought/bought say “aw”, enough/tough say “-uff”, though says “oh”, through says “oo”, and cough says “off”. Same letters, five different songs!

    Worked example

    Example

    Which -ough words rhyme with stuff?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    You need the “-uff” sound family.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Enough and tough — both end with the “-uff” sound, just like stuff. (Through, though and thought do NOT rhyme with stuff!)

    Practice

    Theory

    1Painting pictures with adjectives

    Descriptive adjectives make writing come alive. Instead of the tired words nice, good, big, choose precise, vivid ones: a dazzling firework display, a delicious feast, a colourful parade, a joyful crowd, an enormous dragon, a sparkling river of lanterns. Tip: adjectives usually come before the noun (a colourful costume) or after be (the costume is colourful).

    2English in use

    Boring version: “The party was nice. The food was good and the fireworks were big.” Now watch the adjectives work: “The party was magical! We shared a delicious, steaming feast, admired the dazzling, colourful fireworks, and danced under twinkling lanterns until the sleepy streets went quiet.” Precise, vivid adjectives turn a report into a memory!

    Worked example

    Example

    Upgrade the boring sentence: “The festival was nice. The food was good. The dragon was big.” 🐉

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Swap nice/good/big for three vivid adjectives from this lesson.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “The festival was joyful. The food was delicious. The dragon was enormous!” — three precise pictures instead of three tired words.

    Practice

    Theory

    1If this happens, that always happens

    The zero conditional talks about things that are always true — facts, habits and how the world works. Formula: If + present simple, present simple: “If you don't sleep enough, your brain works slowly.” “If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.” You can swap the halves — then drop the comma: “Your brain works slowly if you don't sleep enough.” You can also use when instead of if: “When I'm tired, I forget things.”

    2English in use

    Brain facts, always true: “If you sleep well, your brain stores what you learned. If you skip breakfast, it works more slowly. When you exercise, more blood flows to your head, and if you practise something every day, it becomes easy. Your brain works slowly if you don't rest it.” Present simple + present simple — because these things happen every single time!

    Worked example

    Example

    Make a zero conditional about the brain: “you exercise / more blood flows to your brain”. 🧠

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    If + present simple, present simple. Both verbs stay in the present.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “If you exercise, more blood flows to your brain.” Always true → both halves use the present simple.

    Practice

    Theory

    1The body team and its jobs

    Each body part has a function (a job): the brain controls the whole body and stores memories; the heart pumps blood; the lungs help you breathe; the stomach digests food; muscles move your bones; the skull is the bony helmet protecting your brain; and nerves carry messages between the brain and the body at amazing speed. Pattern for talking about functions: “The heart's job is to pump blood.” “Nerves are used for carrying messages.”

    2English in use

    Meet the body team! The brain is the boss — it controls everything and stores your memories, safe inside its bony helmet, the skull. The heart's job is to pump blood, the lungs help you breathe, and the stomach digests your lunch. Muscles move your bones, while nerves are used for carrying messages at lightning speed. Every player has a job — and they never take a day off!

    Worked example

    Example

    Match the part to its job: brain / lungs / skull → (protects the brain, controls the body, help you breathe) 🧠

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    One is the boss, one is the bony helmet, one works every time you take a breath.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    The brain controls the body, the lungs help you breathe, and the skull protects the brain.

    Practice

    Theory

    1It’s clever, isn’t it?

    A tag question is a mini-question glued to the end of a sentence to check or agree: “The brain is amazing, isn't it?” The golden rule: positive sentence → negative tag, negative sentence → positive tag. The tag copies the sentence's helper verb: “You can remember it, can't you?” “She doesn't like tests, does she?” If there's no helper, borrow do/does/did: “You forgot your book, didn't you?”

    2English in use

    Chatting after the memory game: “That was fun, wasn't it?” — “Yes! You remembered all ten objects, didn't you?” — “Nine. But you can't beat Mai, can you? She never forgets anything, does she?” — “True. We're playing again tomorrow, aren't we?” Positive flips to negative, negative flips to positive — the little tags keep the conversation bouncing!

    Worked example

    Example

    Add the correct tag: “Your sister remembers every song, ______?”

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Positive sentence → negative tag. No helper verb → borrow does (she = does).
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Your sister remembers every song, doesn't she?” Positive → negative tag, with borrowed does + she.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Reading like a searchlight

    Scanning means moving your eyes quickly over a text to find one specific piece of information — a name, a number, a date — WITHOUT reading every word. How to scan: 1) know exactly what you're looking for; 2) sweep your eyes over the text like a searchlight; 3) stop only when you spot the key word or a number; 4) read just that sentence carefully. Scanning is different from skimming (getting the general idea) and from careful reading (understanding everything).

    2English in use

    Homework: find the year the scientist was born. Did I read the whole three-page article? No! I knew exactly what I was hunting: a 4-digit number. My eyes swept over the text like a searchlight, skipping whole paragraphs, stopping only at numbers… 250 neurons — no… page 2 — no… 1867 — found it! Then I read just that one sentence carefully. Ten seconds. That's scanning — not skimming, not careful reading.

    Worked example

    Example

    Question: “How many neurons does the text mention?” Do you read the whole article slowly, or scan?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    You need ONE number — is careful reading of everything necessary?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Scan! Sweep your eyes for digits or number words, stop at the number, and read just that sentence. One fact = scanning, not careful reading.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Really, so, incredibly!

    Emphasising adverbs turn up the volume of an adjective: The brain is clever → The brain is really clever → incredibly clever! Common ones, from softer to stronger: quite → really / very / so → extremely / incredibly / amazingly. They stand right before the adjective or adverb: “Nerves carry messages amazingly fast.” “The test was so easy!” Careful: don't stack them (“very really so clever” ✗) — one well-chosen adverb is enough.

    2English in use

    My review of the science show: “It was really fun and the host was very funny. The robot demonstration was incredibly clever — the machines moved amazingly fast! The finale was absolutely spectacular, and I was so excited that I couldn't sleep. My little brother found it only quite interesting… he slept through the extremely loud rocket launch!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Make this sentence stronger: “The human brain is powerful.” 🧠

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Slide an emphasising adverb right before “powerful” — pick the strength you want.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “The human brain is incredibly powerful.” (or really / extremely / amazingly powerful — one adverb, right before the adjective.)

    Practice

    Theory

    1Telling others what someone said

    Reporting language lets you pass on someone's words without quoting them exactly. Key verbs: said (that), told + person (that), explained that, asked if/whether. Direct: “The brain never stops working,” said the scientist. → Reported: The scientist said that the brain never stops working. Remember: told ALWAYS needs a person (She told us that… — never “She told that…”), while said doesn't (She said that…).

    2English in use

    Retelling yesterday's science class to Mum: “The teacher said that the brain never stops working, even in sleep. She told us that we should drink more water, and she explained that nerves carry messages faster than a race car. Then she asked if anyone had slept eight hours — and Nam said that he had slept ten!” Mum laughed and told me that Nam is her kind of scientist.

    Worked example

    Example

    Report this sentence: The teacher: “Sleep helps your memory.” 😴

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Use “The teacher said that…” or “The teacher told us that…”.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “The teacher said that sleep helps your memory.” or “The teacher told us that sleep helps our memory.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1Glue words for sentences

    Connectives glue ideas together so your story flows. Adding: and, also, as well as. Contrasting: but, however, although. Cause and result: because (gives the reason), so (gives the result): “The dragon was hungry, so it flew to the village.” “The knight hid because the dragon was enormous.” Time: while, when, after, before. Choose the connective that matches the JOB the sentence is doing.

    2English in use

    A mini story, glued together: “The dragon was hungry, so it flew to the village. The knight hid because the dragon was enormous, but the baker did not run. Although she was afraid, she offered the dragon fresh bread and a pot of honey. While the dragon ate, it began to purr, and after that day, the village had a very large, very loyal guard.”

    Worked example

    Example

    Join with because or so: “It started to rain. The picnic moved inside.” 🌧️

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Rain is the REASON; moving inside is the RESULT. Because introduces reasons; so introduces results.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “It started to rain, so the picnic moved inside.” — or — “The picnic moved inside because it started to rain.” Both are correct: so → result, because → reason.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Story families

    Stories come in types (genres), each with its own flavour: a fairy tale (magic, princes, “Once upon a time…”), a fable (animals that act like people + a lesson/moral, like Aesop's tortoise and hare), a legend (an old story about a hero, possibly based on truth — like the legend of Lake Hoan Kiem), a myth (explains the world with gods and magic), an adventure story (exciting journeys and danger), and science fiction (future worlds, space, robots). Knowing the type helps you predict what will happen!

    2English in use

    Tour of my bookshelf! “Once upon a time, a princess…” — that's my fairy tale. The tortoise beating the hare, with a lesson at the end — a classic fable. The sword returned to the turtle of Hoan Kiem Lake — our beloved legend. A story of gods explaining why the sea is salty — a myth. Robots on Mars in year 3000 — science fiction. And a dangerous jungle journey? Pure adventure!

    Worked example

    Example

    A story starts: “A greedy fox tricked a crow into dropping its cheese — and learned nothing is free.” What type of story is it? 🧀

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Talking animals + a lesson at the end…
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    A fable — animals acting like people plus a moral (lesson) is the classic fable recipe, just like Aesop's stories.

    Practice

    Theory

    1When pictures speak

    A symbol is a picture or sign that carries a meaning without words: ♥ means love, ☂ warns of rain, a skull on a bottle means danger, and a dove stands for peace. Stories and books use symbols too: a map in an adventure book uses ⛰ and ✕ (“X marks the spot”); traffic signs “speak” to drivers; and in stories, objects can be symbols — a key can stand for a secret, winter can stand for sadness. Reading symbols is reading meaning without words!

    2English in use

    Reading a whole story with zero words! On the treasure map, ⛰ means mountains, the wavy lines mean a river, and the big ✕ marks the spot. On the path, a skull sign warns danger, a red light commands stop, and at the journey's end a dove and a ♥ promise peace and love. Symbols speak every language at once — you just read the pictures.

    Worked example

    Example

    On a treasure map you see: a ⛰ symbol, a wavy-lines symbol, and a big ✕. What does the map “say”?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Mountains… water… and the most famous map symbol of all!
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    ⛰ = mountains, the wavy lines = a river or the sea, and ✕ marks where the treasure is buried — the map tells a whole story without a single word.

    Practice

    Theory

    1The long action and the interruption

    Stories love this team: the past continuous (was/were + verb-ing) paints the long background action, and the past simple is the short action that interrupts it: “I was reading a ghost story when the lights went out!” Pattern: While + past continuous, past simple — or — past simple + when + past continuous… Actually remember it simply: long action = was/were -ing, sudden event = past simple: “While the giant was sleeping, Jack stole the golden hen.”

    2English in use

    The scariest page of my book: “I was reading a ghost story when the lights suddenly went out. Rain was tapping on the window while the wind was howling outside. Then, while I was hiding under my blanket, something jumped onto the bed! I screamed… and the cat purred.” Long background actions in -ing, sudden events in past simple — that's how stories build suspense!

    Worked example

    Example

    Combine into one story sentence: (the children / play in the garden — long action) + (it / start to rain — sudden event) 🌧️

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Long action → were playing; sudden event → started. Join them with when or while.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “The children were playing in the garden when it started to rain.” (or: “While the children were playing…, it started to rain.”)

    Practice

    Theory

    1Tiny sentences, big wisdom

    A proverb is a short, well-known saying that carries wisdom or advice: “Practice makes perfect.” “Don't judge a book by its cover” (don't judge by looks). “Actions speak louder than words.” “Slow and steady wins the race” (from the tortoise and hare fable!). Proverbs usually have a hidden meaning — “Don't judge a book by its cover” isn't really about books. Vietnamese has proverbs too: Có công mài sắt, có ngày nên kim is a cousin of “Practice makes perfect”!

    2English in use

    A letter to my cousin: “Dear Bi, don't quit the guitar after one hard week — practice makes perfect, and remember the tortoise: slow and steady wins the race. Don't worry that your old guitar looks plain; don't judge a book by its cover! And instead of promising to practise, just do it — actions speak louder than words. As Grandma says: có công mài sắt, có ngày nên kim!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Your friend gives up the piano after two days: “It's too hard!” Which proverb fits, and what does it mean? 🎹

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Think of the proverb about practising… or the tortoise!
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Practice makes perfect” — keep practising and you will improve. (“Slow and steady wins the race” works too: small steady steps beat giving up.)

    Practice

    Theory

    1Making characters talk

    Direct speech shows a character's exact words inside quotation marks (“ ”): “I'm not afraid of the dark,” said Mai bravely. The rules: the exact words go inside “ ”; a comma (or ? or !) separates the speech from the speaker tag; the speech starts with a capital letter; and start a new line for each new speaker. Vary the speech verbs to show feeling: whispered, shouted, laughed, cried, asked — much livelier than “said, said, said”.

    2English in use

    A scene with the punctuation spotlight on:
    “Where is the treasure?” asked the pirate.
    “Follow the map,” whispered the parrot, looking around nervously.
    “Watch out for the dragon!” shouted the guard from the tower.
    “I'm not afraid,” laughed the pirate. — Quotation marks around the exact words, a comma or ?/! before the closing mark, a capital letter to start, a new line for each speaker — and not a single boring “said”!

    Worked example

    Example

    Punctuate this direct speech: watch out for the dragon shouted the guard 🐉

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Quotation marks around the exact words, a capital letter to start, and an exclamation mark for shouting!
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Watch out for the dragon!” shouted the guard. — capital W, “ ” around the words, and ! for the shout.

    Practice

    Theory

    1As brave as a lion

    A simile compares two things using as … as or like to paint a vivid picture: “The knight was as brave as a lion.” “Her smile shone like the sun.” “The baby slept like a log” (very deeply). Classic similes: as quiet as a mouse, as fast as lightning, as cold as ice, as busy as a bee. Similes make stories and poems sparkle — instead of “he ran fast”, write “he ran like the wind!”

    2English in use

    My grandfather, in similes: “He is as strong as an ox but as gentle as a lamb. In the morning he moves like a sleepy bear, yet at chess his mind is as fast as lightning. His laugh booms like thunder, his hands are as rough as tree bark from years of work — and when he tells stories, the whole house goes as quiet as a mouse.”

    Worked example

    Example

    Finish the simile to describe a very quiet library: “The library was as quiet as ______.” 📚

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Which tiny animal is famous for being silent?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “The library was as quiet as a mouse.” (Your own creative endings work too: as quiet as falling snow!)

    Practice

    Theory

    1Talking about long, long ago

    To discuss ancient history, we use the past simple plus special time language: thousands of years ago, in ancient times, around 2500 BCE, centuries ago. Useful sentence starters: “The ancient Egyptians built the pyramids thousands of years ago.” “The Romans used to build long, straight roads.” “Life was very different in ancient times — there was no electricity!” Note used to + verb for repeated past habits: Roman children used to play with wooden toys.

    2English in use

    From my history notebook: “Thousands of years ago, the ancient Egyptians built the pyramids beside the Nile. In ancient times, Egyptian farmers used to plant crops after the river's floods, and Roman children used to play with wooden toys. Life was very different — there was no electricity, and the fastest ‘car’ was a horse! Around 2,000 years ago, Roman engineers made roads so straight and strong that some still exist today.”

    Worked example

    Example

    Talk about ancient Egypt using “used to”: (Egyptian farmers / plant crops beside the Nile River every year)

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    A repeated past habit → used to + base verb.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Egyptian farmers used to plant crops beside the Nile River every year — the river's floods made the soil rich.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1I think… because…

    To share an opinion politely, open with an opinion phrase — I think (that)…, In my opinion…, I believe…, To me,… — and then give a reason with because: “I think the pyramids are more amazing than the Colosseum because they are much older.” To agree: “I agree with you.” “That's a good point.” To disagree politely: “I see what you mean, but…” “I'm not sure I agree, because…” An opinion + a reason is always stronger than an opinion alone!

    2English in use

    Classroom debate — Rome or Egypt? “In my opinion, ancient Egypt is more fascinating because of the pyramids and the mummies,” said Lan. “That's a good point,” replied Nam, “and I agree the pyramids are amazing. But I see what you mean, and still, I think Rome wins, because Roman roads and the Colosseum survive after 2,000 years!” — “I'm not sure I agree… but what a great debate!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Give an opinion with a reason: Which would you rather visit — ancient Rome or ancient Egypt?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Opinion phrase + choice + because + reason.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “In my opinion, ancient Egypt would be more exciting to visit because I could see the pyramids being built and sail on the Nile!” (Any choice works — the reason is what matters.)

    Practice

    Theory

    1Commands and instructions

    The imperative gives commands, instructions or advice. Just use the base verb — no subject: “Look at this ancient coin!” “Walk this way to the temple.” “Be careful near the ruins.” Negative: Don't + verb: “Don't touch the mummy!” Make it polite with please: “Please follow the guide.” Imperatives power museum signs (“Do not touch”), recipes (“Mix the flour”), directions (“Turn left”) and warnings (“Watch out!”).

    2English in use

    Museum guide, speaking to the group: “Welcome! Please follow me and stay together. Look at this 3,000-year-old mummy — but don't touch the glass, and don't use flash on your cameras. Be careful on the old stairs, turn left at the golden statue, and listen for the gong. Hungry? Try the café — and please don't feed the pigeons at the entrance!”

    Worked example

    Example

    You are a museum guide. Give the visitors one positive instruction and one negative rule.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Positive: base verb (+ please). Negative: Don't + verb.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Please stay with the group.” + “Don't use flash when you photograph the paintings.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1One root, many relatives

    A word family is a group of words built from the same root: history → historian (person) → historic/historical (adjective); build → builder → building; discover → discovery → discoverer; explore → explorer → exploration. Common suffixes: -er/-or/-ian = a person who does it; -tion/-y = the thing or action; -ic/-ical/-ful = the adjective. Knowing one family member helps you understand the whole family!

    2English in use

    One root, a whole family at work: “The historian wrote a historical book about history's greatest discovery. An explorer led the exploration that discovered the tomb, and the discoverer became famous overnight. Roman builders could build buildings that still stand — truly historic work!” Spot the suffixes: -ian and -er for people, -tion and -y for things, -ic and -ical for adjectives.

    Worked example

    Example

    Complete the family of explore: person = ______, the activity = ______. Use them in a sentence about Egypt.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Person → -er; activity → -ation.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Explorer, exploration: “The explorer led an exploration deep into the pharaoh's tomb.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1In, on, at — and where things stand

    Time: in + months/years/centuries (in 79 CE, in July); on + days/dates (on Monday, on 15th March); at + clock times (at noon, at 7 o'clock). Location & position: in (inside: in the tomb), on (touching a surface: on the wall), at (a point: at the gate), plus next to, between, behind, in front of, under, above: “The sphinx sits in front of the pyramid.” “The treasure lay under the floor, between two columns.”

    2English in use

    Museum visit plan: “The Egypt exhibition opens at 9 o'clock on Saturday. Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE — that room is on the second floor. Meet me at the main gate, in front of the sphinx statue, which sits between two tall columns. The mummy lies in a glass case, the paintings hang on the walls, and — legend says — a secret door hides under the stairs, right behind the gift shop!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Fill the three gaps: “The museum opens ______ 9 o'clock ______ Saturdays, and the mummy room is ______ the second floor.” 🏺

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Clock time → at; days → on; a floor is a surface → on.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “The museum opens at 9 o'clock on Saturdays, and the mummy room is on the second floor.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1Will, might, probably

    A prediction is a guess about the future. Show HOW sure you are: very sure → will / won't (“It will rain in the rainforest today — it rains almost every day!”); quite sure → will probably (“We will probably see monkeys.”); not sure → might / may (“We might see a jaguar, but they hide very well.”). Before reading a book, good readers also predict: “I think this story will be about a lost explorer, because of the cover picture.”

    2English in use

    Packing for the rainforest trip: “It will be hot and humid — rainforests always are — and it will definitely rain, so I'm bringing a raincoat. We will probably see monkeys and colourful parrots near the camp. We might hear a howler monkey, and if we're very lucky we may spot a sloth — but we probably won't see a jaguar, because they hide too well. I think it will be the best trip of my life!”

    Worked example

    Example

    You are packing for a rainforest trip. Make two predictions: one you are SURE about, one you are NOT sure about. 🌧️

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Sure → will; not sure → might.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “It will be hot and humid” (sure — rainforests always are) + “We might hear a howler monkey” (not sure — you need luck!).

    Practice

    Theory

    1The rainforest orchestra

    The rainforest is full of sounds, and English has a word for each: birds sing and chirp, parrots squawk, monkeys howl, frogs croak, insects buzz, snakes hiss, leaves rustle in the wind, rain patters on the leaves, thunder rumbles, and waterfalls roar. Many sound words imitate the actual sound (buzz! hiss!) — this is called onomatopoeia. Sound words make descriptions come alive: “Leaves rustled, frogs croaked, and somewhere far away a waterfall roared.”

    2English in use

    Dawn in the rainforest — close your eyes and listen: birds chirp and sing in the canopy while parrots squawk overhead. Insects buzz past your ear, frogs croak by the stream, and a snake hisses somewhere in the leaves that rustle in the wind. Rain begins to patter, thunder rumbles far away, monkeys howl — and behind it all, the great waterfall roars. A whole orchestra of onomatopoeia!

    Worked example

    Example

    You close your eyes in the rainforest and hear: vo ve… phì phì… xào xạc. Write the three English sound verbs and their makers. 🌧️

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    An insect, a snake, and the leaves…
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Insects buzz, snakes hiss, and leaves rustle — three players in the rainforest orchestra!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Have you ever…?

    The present perfect = have/has + past participle (the 3rd verb form): “I have visited the national park.” “She has seen a monkey.” Use it for life experiences without an exact time: “Have you ever climbed a mountain?” “I have never touched a snake!” Key participles: go → gone/been, see → seen, eat → eaten, do → done, visit → visited. Compare: past simple names WHEN (I saw a toucan yesterday); present perfect doesn't (I have seen a toucan — some time in my life).

    2English in use

    Travel interview with Grandpa: “Have you ever climbed a mountain?” — “Yes, I have! I have climbed Fansipan twice.” — “Have you ever seen a wild elephant?” — “No, I haven't. I have never seen one — but I have ridden a buffalo, I have eaten crocodile soup, and I have visited ten countries. Yesterday I just visited the market, though!” — spot how the exact time switches him to past simple!

    Worked example

    Example

    Ask a friend about a life experience with “Have you ever…?” and give both possible short answers.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Have you ever + past participle…? → Yes, I have. / No, I haven't (never).
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Have you ever seen a waterfall?” → “Yes, I have!” or “No, I haven't — I have never seen one.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1Quite, very, extremely

    Adverbs of degree measure HOW MUCH — like a volume dial from low to high: slightly / a bit → quite / fairly → very / really → extremely / incredibly. Same fact, different strengths: “The understorey is quite dark.” “The canopy is very noisy.” “The forest floor is extremely humid.” Choosing precisely matters: a jaguar is not just “quite fast” — it is extremely fast; drizzle is not “extremely wet” — it is only slightly wet.

    2English in use

    Rainforest weather report: “This morning it is slightly cooler than yesterday — just one degree. The understorey is quite dark and fairly quiet, but the canopy above is very noisy and really busy. By noon it will be extremely hot and incredibly humid — the jaguars, who are amazingly fast, will nap through it all. Turn the volume dial: slightly → quite → very → extremely!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Put in order from WEAKEST to STRONGEST: extremely hot — slightly hot — very hot — quite hot.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Think of the volume dial: hơi → khá → rất → cực kỳ.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    slightly hot → quite hot → very hot → extremely hot — the dial turns from a warm morning to rainforest noon!

    Practice

    Theory

    1Information at a glance

    A fact file presents information about one topic in a quick, organised way: a title, a picture, and short headed sections — for an animal: Name, Habitat, Diet, Size, Special skill, Fun fact. Fact files use short phrases and the present simple (facts!): “Diet: insects and fruit. Habitat: the canopy of South American rainforests.” They are perfect for posters, projects and quick research — a reader can scan them in seconds.

    2English in use

    SLOTH — fact file. Habitat: canopy trees of Central and South American rainforests. Diet: leaves, buds and soft twigs. Size: about as big as a small dog. Special skill: moving in super slow motion — and swimming surprisingly well! Fun fact: sloths sleep up to 15 hours a day, and tiny green algae grow on their fur. — Title, headings, short present-simple phrases: scannable in seconds!

    Worked example

    Example

    Build a mini fact file for the sloth using these notes: lives in canopy trees / eats leaves / moves very slowly / sleeps up to 15 hours a day. 🦥

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Sort the notes under headings: Habitat, Diet, Special skill, Fun fact.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    SLOTH — Habitat: canopy trees. Diet: leaves. Special skill: moving in super slow motion. Fun fact: sleeps up to 15 hours a day!

    Practice

    Theory

    1A beautiful small green frog

    When several adjectives describe one noun, English lines them up in a fixed order: opinion → size → age → colour → material/origin + noun: “a beautiful small green frog”, “an amazing huge old tree”, “a long brown wooden canoe”. That's why “a green small beautiful frog” sounds wrong to English ears! Memory trick: your OPINION comes first (beautiful, amazing), facts follow (size, age, colour), and what it's made of hugs the noun (wooden canoe).

    OpinionSizeAgeColourMaterialNoun
    beautifulsmall—green—frog
    amazinghugeold——tree
    —long—brownwoodencanoe

    2English in use

    Souvenir shopping in the rainforest village: “I bought a beautiful small green frog carving, a lovely tiny red bead bracelet, and an amazing huge old map of the river. Dad chose a long brown wooden canoe paddle, and Mum found a gorgeous soft blue cotton scarf.” Opinion → size → age → colour → material — every single time, and that's why it all sounds right!

    Worked example

    Example

    Put in the correct order: “frog / red / tiny / lovely” + a. 🐸

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Opinion → size → colour → noun.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “a lovely tiny red frog” — opinion (lovely), size (tiny), colour (red), noun (frog).

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is it like?

    Like compares one thing to another: “The rainforest air feels like a warm wet blanket.” “A toucan's beak looks like a banana!” Ask about qualities with What is … like?: “What's the rainforest like?” → “It's hot, noisy and full of life.” Pattern: look like / sound like / feel like / smell like + noun: “Howler monkeys sound like roaring lions.” Careful: this comparing “like” is different from the verb like (= enjoy): “I like mangoes” vs “This fruit tastes like a mango.”

    2English in use

    “What's the rainforest like?” asked my friend. “It's hot, noisy and full of life! The air feels like a warm wet blanket, and the vines hang like green ropes. A toucan's beak looks like a giant banana, howler monkeys sound like roaring lions, and the rain on the leaves smells like a fresh garden. I like it there — but careful: that last ‘like’ means enjoy, not compare!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Answer with a comparison: “What does a howler monkey sound like?” 🐒

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    sound like + a famous loud thing.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “A howler monkey sounds like a roaring lion — you can hear it kilometres away!”

    Practice

    Theory

    1Two words, one new thing

    A compound noun joins two words into one new meaning: rain + forest = rainforest, wild + life = wildlife, butter + fly = butterfly, jelly + fish = jellyfish, sea + horse = seahorse, grass + hopper = grasshopper. Some are written as one word (ladybird), some as two (polar bear), some with a hyphen. The FIRST word usually describes the second: a seahorse is a kind of “horse” of the sea — not a sea for horses! Compound nouns are everywhere in the animal kingdom.

    2English in use

    Nature-walk diary, built from word pairs: “We hiked through the rainforest to see the wildlife. A butterfly landed on my hat, a grasshopper jumped across the path, and a ladybird crawled up my sleeve. At the waterfall we ate lunch, and in the rock pool below — unbelievable! — my sister spotted a tiny seahorse. Even a jellyfish drifted by. Two words, one new creature, everywhere we looked!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Build three animal compound nouns from these pieces: jelly / sea / grass + fish / horse / hopper. 🐟

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Match each first word to its partner: what swims like jelly? what looks like a tiny horse? what hops in the grass?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Jellyfish (sứa), seahorse (cá ngựa), grasshopper (châu chấu) — three animals built from word pairs!

    Practice

    Theory

    1In danger, at risk, under threat

    Some prepositions and nouns form fixed teams you must learn together: in danger (Tigers are in danger.), at risk (Their habitat is at risk.), under threat (Rainforests are under threat.), in the wild (Pandas live in the wild and in zoos.), on Earth (the largest animal on Earth), in captivity (kept by people, e.g. in a zoo). These fixed pairs never change their preposition — “on danger” or “at the wild” sound wrong to every English ear!

    2English in use

    From our conservation poster: “The saola lives in the wild only in the Annamite Mountains — and it is in danger. Its forest home is at risk from cutting, and ancient trees everywhere are under threat. Some animals now survive only in captivity, but every creature on Earth deserves a safe home in nature. Fixed word-teams for a fixed promise: protect them!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Complete the conservation sentence: “Saola live ______ the wild in Vietnam, but they are ______ danger.” 🦌

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Both fixed pairs use the same little preposition here!
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “Saola live in the wild in Vietnam, but they are in danger.” — in the wild, in danger: fixed teams.

    Practice

    Theory

    1It, its and the troublemaker it's

    It stands for one animal or thing: “The saola is rare. It lives in the Annamite Mountains.” Its (NO apostrophe) shows belonging: “The peacock spreads its tail.” “The cat licked its paw.” The troublemaker: it's (WITH apostrophe) is short for it is / it has: “It's a shy animal.” (= It is). Test: if you can replace the word with “it is”, write it's; if it shows possession, write its. “It's hunting its prey.” — both in one sentence!

    2English in use

    The octopus, star of my report: “It's one of the cleverest animals in the sea. It has three hearts, and its blood is blue! When it's in danger, it changes its colour in less than a second and hides its soft body between the rocks. It's amazing — and yes, it's been tested: every apostrophe here can be replaced by ‘it is’ or ‘it has’!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Choose its or it's: “______ amazing how the octopus changes ______ colour!” 🐙

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Try the test: can you say “It is amazing”? Can you say “it is colour”?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “It's amazing how the octopus changes its colour!” — It's = it is; its = belonging to the octopus.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Enjoy watching vs want to watch

    After some verbs comes a gerund (verb-ing); after others, an infinitive (to + verb). Gerund team: enjoy, love, like, hate, finish, keep + -ing: “I enjoy watching wildlife documentaries.” “The monkeys kept climbing.” Infinitive team: want, hope, decide, plan, need, would like + to + verb: “We want to protect endangered animals.” “She hopes to see a saola one day.” Learn each verb's team — “enjoy to watch” and “want watching” both sound wrong!

    2English in use

    Our wildlife club plan: “We all enjoy watching birds and love drawing them, so this term we want to protect the ones in the school garden. We have decided to build three nest boxes and we hope to finish before the rainy season. Mai keeps reminding everyone to bring wood, Nam hates getting up early but plans to come anyway — and we all would like to see the first chicks in spring!”

    Worked example

    Example

    Complete both halves: “I enjoy ______ (draw) animals, and I want ______ (become) a wildlife artist.”

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    enjoy → gerund team; want → infinitive team.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    “I enjoy drawing animals, and I want to become a wildlife artist.”

    Practice

    Theory

    1A little paper with a big message

    A leaflet is a small printed page that informs or persuades — like “Save Our Sea Turtles!”. Ingredients: a big catchy title; subheadings to organise; short paragraphs and bullet points (easy to scan); pictures; persuasive language — imperatives (“Join us!” “Don't drop litter!”), questions to the reader (“Did you know…?”), and strong adjectives; plus a call to action at the end telling readers exactly what to do (“Visit our website — Volunteer this Sunday!”).

    2English in use

    SAVE OUR SEA TURTLES — BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE!
    Did you know that baby turtles follow the moonlight to find the sea?
    • Sea turtles are in danger from plastic and bright lights.
    • One beach clean-up can save a whole nest!
    Don't drop litter. Turn off beach lights at night. Join us!
    👉 Act now: beach clean-up, this Sunday, 7 a.m. — every helper counts! — Catchy title ✓ question ✓ bullets ✓ imperatives ✓ call to action ✓: a complete leaflet!

    Worked example

    Example

    Write the title and call to action for a leaflet about protecting street cats in your neighbourhood. 🐱

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    Title: short + catchy (maybe an imperative!). Call to action: tell readers EXACTLY what to do.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Title: “Paws in Need — Help Our Street Cats!” Call to action: “Leave clean water outside your door, and join our feeding team every Saturday at 8 a.m.!”

    Chant (đọc theo nhịp): Cả lớp đọc bài vần theo nhịp.

    slightly
    hơi, một chút

    It is slightly cooler this morning.

    Slightly (hơi): Sáng nay trời hơi mát hơn.

    quite
    khá

    The understorey is quite dark.

    Quite (khá): Tầng dưới tán khá tối.

    fairly
    tương đối

    The stream is fairly quiet today.

    Fairly (tương đối): Con suối hôm nay tương đối yên ắng.

    degree
    mức độ

    Adverbs of degree measure how much.

    Degree (mức độ): Trạng từ mức độ đo lường bao nhiêu.

    mild
    nhẹ, dịu

    The weather stays mild in the shade.

    Mild (dịu nhẹ): Thời tiết dịu mát trong bóng râm.

    intense
    dữ dội, gay gắt

    The noon heat is intense.

    Intense (gay gắt): Cái nóng buổi trưa thật gay gắt.

    barely
    hầu như không

    I could barely hear the whisper.

    Barely (hầu như không): Tôi hầu như không nghe được tiếng thì thầm.

    nearly
    gần như

    The bottle is nearly empty.

    Nearly (gần như): Chai nước gần cạn.

    The 8 important English words of lesson 8.5 — Fact files, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence.

    fact
    sự thật, dữ kiện

    A fact file lists facts under headings.

    Fact (dữ kiện): Fact file liệt kê dữ kiện theo đề mục.

    file
    hồ sơ, phiếu

    Build a fact file about the sloth.

    File (phiếu/hồ sơ): Hãy lập phiếu thông tin về con lười.

    habitat
    môi trường sống

    Habitat: canopy trees of the rainforest.

    Habitat (môi trường sống): Nơi sống: cây tầng tán rừng mưa.

    diet
    chế độ ăn

    Diet: leaves, buds and soft twigs.

    Diet (chế độ ăn): Thức ăn: lá, chồi non và cành mềm.

    size
    kích thước

    Size: about as big as a small dog.

    Size (kích thước): Cỡ một chú chó nhỏ.

    skill
    kỹ năng

    Special skill: swimming surprisingly well!

    Skill (kỹ năng): Kỹ năng đặc biệt: bơi giỏi bất ngờ!

    heading
    đề mục

    Headings make facts easy to find.

    Heading (đề mục): Đề mục giúp tìm thông tin dễ dàng.

    poster
    áp phích

    Turn your fact file into a poster.

    Poster (áp phích): Biến fact file thành một tấm áp phích.

    The 8 important English words of lesson 8.6 — Adjective order, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence.

    wooden
    bằng gỗ

    We paddled a long brown wooden canoe.

    Wooden (bằng gỗ): Chúng tôi chèo chiếc xuồng gỗ nâu, dài.

    golden
    bằng vàng, vàng óng

    She found a tiny golden key.

    Golden (vàng óng): Cô bé tìm thấy chiếc chìa khóa vàng bé xíu.

    tiny
    bé xíu

    A lovely tiny red frog sat there.

    Tiny (bé xíu): Một chú ếch đỏ bé xíu đáng yêu ngồi đó.

    huge
    khổng lồ

    An amazing huge old tree shaded us.

    Huge (khổng lồ): Một cây cổ thụ khổng lồ tuyệt diệu che mát chúng tôi.

    lovely
    đáng yêu

    What a lovely little bracelet!

    Lovely (đáng yêu): Chiếc vòng tay nhỏ đáng yêu làm sao!

    cotton
    bằng vải cotton

    Mum chose a soft blue cotton scarf.

    Cotton (vải cotton): Mẹ chọn chiếc khăn cotton xanh mềm mại.

    leather
    bằng da

    Dad bought an old brown leather bag.

    Leather (bằng da): Bố mua chiếc túi da nâu cũ.

    silk
    lụa

    The gorgeous red silk dress shone.

    Silk (lụa): Chiếc váy lụa đỏ lộng lẫy ánh lên.

    blanket
    chiếc chăn

    The air feels like a warm wet blanket.

    Blanket (chiếc chăn): Không khí như một chiếc chăn ấm và ẩm.

    beak
    mỏ chim

    A toucan's beak looks like a banana.

    Beak (mỏ chim): Mỏ toucan trông như quả chuối.

    fur
    bộ lông thú

    The jaguar's fur glows like sunlight.

    Fur (bộ lông): Bộ lông báo đốm ánh lên như nắng.

    stripes
    sọc vằn

    The tiger's stripes look like shadows.

    Stripes (sọc vằn): Sọc vằn của hổ trông như những vệt bóng.

    glow
    phát sáng, ánh lên

    Fireflies glow like tiny lanterns.

    Glow (phát sáng): Đom đóm sáng như những chiếc đèn lồng tí hon.

    drift
    trôi lững lờ

    Clouds drift like sleepy sheep.

    Drift (trôi lững lờ): Mây trôi như đàn cừu ngái ngủ.

    silky
    mượt như lụa

    The petals feel silky and soft.

    Silky (mượt như lụa): Cánh hoa mượt mà, mềm mại.

    spiky
    tua tủa gai

    The durian is spiky like a hedgehog!

    Spiky (tua tủa gai): Quả sầu riêng gai góc như chú nhím!

    rainforest
    rừng mưa nhiệt đới

    Rain + forest = rainforest!

    Rainforest (rừng mưa): Rain + forest = rainforest!

    wildlife
    động vật hoang dã

    The park protects local wildlife.

    Wildlife (động vật hoang dã): Công viên bảo vệ động vật hoang dã địa phương.

    butterfly
    bươm bướm

    A butterfly landed on my hat.

    Butterfly (bươm bướm): Một chú bướm đậu lên mũ tôi.

    jellyfish
    con sứa

    A jellyfish drifted by the rocks.

    Jellyfish (con sứa): Một con sứa trôi qua ghềnh đá.

    seahorse
    cá ngựa

    My sister spotted a tiny seahorse!

    Seahorse (cá ngựa): Em gái tôi phát hiện một chú cá ngựa tí hon!

    grasshopper
    châu chấu

    A grasshopper jumped across the path.

    Grasshopper (châu chấu): Một chú châu chấu nhảy ngang lối đi.

    waterfall
    thác nước

    We ate lunch at the waterfall.

    Waterfall (thác nước): Chúng tôi ăn trưa bên thác nước.

    ladybird
    bọ rùa

    A ladybird crawled up my sleeve.

    Ladybird (bọ rùa): Một chú bọ rùa bò lên tay áo tôi.
